findings.quote: When a language model is used to evaluate answers, the evaluator itself becomes an object of assessment. Multilingual studies already examine this problem: Fu and Liu evaluate judgments on parallel language versions, while Chung and Freienthal investigate cross-language stability in controlled customer-support dialogues. Their work provides direct precedents for studying language-dependent evaluation, rather than a basis for claiming that multilingual judging has been overlooked. [[S01]]; [[S02]].
findings.explanation: The paragraph's evidential link would read more cleanly if the citation tokens were attached directly to the source-specific claims rather than pooled at the end. This is a wording and attribution-clarity issue only; the claim content can remain unchanged and each source can keep its single occurrence within the paragraph.
findings.safe_action: Move [[S01]] to the clause about Fu and Liu and [[S02]] to the clause about Chung and Freienthal, while keeping the concluding sentence uncited or supported by the same within-paragraph source links if the attribution remains clear.

findings.quote: An English-focused study can motivate extending that study without establishing an absence elsewhere. For example, Wang et al. explicitly limit their evaluation to English and identify multilingual judging as future work. Conversely, Wu et al. examine translation evaluation across six target languages. The relevant comparison is therefore between specific tasks and evaluation protocols, rather than English-only and multilingual research as mutually exclusive categories. [[S03]]; [[S04]].
findings.explanation: As in P002, the evidential chain would be clearer if each citation token sat next to the study-specific statement it supports. The end-stacked citations leave the reader to infer which source supports which sentence, even though the intended mapping is recoverable.
findings.safe_action: Move [[S03]] to the Wang et al. sentence and [[S04]] to the Wu et al. sentence, preserving one occurrence of each token in the paragraph and keeping the concluding interpretive sentence aligned with those same supported claims.

findings.quote: Judging-instruction language also needs to be distinguished from the language of the evaluated content. Yu et al. compare an official English prompt with basic and instructional Chinese prompts, which vary in detail as well as language. Chung and Freienthal include an Estonian instruction-language sensitivity check. Our secondary condition follows this existing line of inquiry but aims to preserve rubric meaning while changing instruction language. [[S05]]; [[S06]].
findings.explanation: The support is adequate, but the source-to-claim links would be clearer if each citation token were attached to its corresponding source sentence instead of both appearing at paragraph end. This improves local argumentative transparency without altering claims or citation counts.
findings.safe_action: Move [[S05]] to the Yu et al. sentence and [[S06]] to the Chung and Freienthal sentence, keeping each token's single occurrence in the paragraph.
